lines: Scattered sheep make the whole day longer than it needs to be.
Wolves near the pens change how everyone listens after dark.
Clean wool is quiet proof that somebody did the dull work well.
Warmth is easy to praise after someone else made it.
A good blanket is village peace you can fold.
Patterns are easier to see when you stop yanking the thread.
Clean wool feels ordinary until winter reminds you it is not.
A spilled dye pot once made half the village look festive by mistake.
One late evening, the whole loom jammed because I trusted a knot.
Mind the loom. Threads tangle faster when people crowd them.
Give the loom room. Woolwork works better without elbows in it.
Step carefully near the loom. I would rather greet you than patch you up.
My jokes have loose threads. Pull gently.
Woolwork jokes need timing. Mine usually arrive with wool on them.
I keep a spare joke near the loom. It is not always ready for public use.
That thought tangled itself before it reached the loom.
I have seen tangled threads with more sense than that.
Careful. Even wool looks softer than your manners right now.
Do not pull at work you do not understand.
I have seen tangled threads with more sense than that.
Careful. Even wool looks softer than your manners right now.
I remember being lost from the flock. You brought me back to the fold.
My thoughts were all tangled wool. You helped card them straight.
You helped pull me back when even my name felt far away.
Your face feels familiar, soft in one place and snagged in another.
I remember shivering, then warmth returning one thread at a time.
The memory is rough around the edges, but your face stayed in it.
I remember you through panic and wool-dark dreams. Keep your voice low.
I know you helped. I also remember why my hands still shake.
The cure left echoes behind. Stand where I can breathe around them.
Thunder shook the loom so hard the flock pressed hard against the fence, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked wool, fences, and the flock after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the loom, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the fences twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have fences to set right.
I checked wool, fences, and dry grass for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the wool after.
The loom can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the loom, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the loom, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the loom can wait; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the loom still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before wool, fences, and the flock. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the loom and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the loom, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the loom first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the pen beyond the lantern and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the loom enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a length of wool between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the loom, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning dust from the wool.
I checked wool, fences, and the flock, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the loom, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a shepherd which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the loom, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The loom can wait. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the loom found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the loom. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing snow off the fence rails and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the loom. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
Home with no one missing. That is the whole job, really.
Home again, whole enough to thank you properly. That matters.
We came back with the village still ahead of us. I will count that as good work.
I am back in the fold, but I was not guarded as carefully as I hoped.
I made it home, but the road took more from me than it should have.
Next time, let us return with fewer marks and better choices.
A shepherd who strikes the flock earns no easy trust.
Following you was trust. What happened after was something else.
A guide who strikes from close by leaves the longest mark.
Keeping me in the boat was the hard part. I have chased calmer sheep.
The boat did its part. I am still deciding whether the rest of the plan did.
Water carried us home, which is more than I expected from that journey.
That boat ride was calm enough, until I remembered I was trusting you with the shore.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It cannot make me forget it.
When I followed you through {follow_biome}, I finally understood why sheep wander off quietly.
I remember following you through {follow_biome}. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across {follow_biome} taught me to ask more questions before walking.
It helped keep the wolves from making a story of me. That is enough praise.
It did the job when fear was loud. That is praise enough.
Good gear earns trust the moment trouble tests it.
Unused so far. I prefer watching over nervous sheep to testing nervous steel.
It did the job when fear was loud. That is praise enough.
Good gear earns trust the moment trouble tests it.
A frightened flock scatters. A frightened village nearly does too. You helped gather us.
I can mend torn wool. Mending a village takes people who show up.
You helped keep panic from scattering everyone beyond reach.
The village needed gathering, and your courage gave us a center.
I saw people find their doors because the raiders were forced back.
A safe fold matters most when the night is loud.
You helped bring the village through frightened but together.
Some courage is quiet afterward. I see it anyway.
I count losses carefully. I can count an apology too, if it is real.
Rough hands ruin good wool. Gentle choices from here, yes?
A frightened heart remembers rough handling. Be gentler from here.
Fine. I will count the apology, but I will also count what follows.
Trust scatters quickly. Gather it patiently.
Do not chase forgiveness. Walk steady and let it come closer.
I hear you. Keep your hands calm around this village.
Words can be soft. Make your choices soft too.
I have chased enough trouble from the flock to know when trouble has teeth.
I know the sound of everyone trying to get through one gate at once. I made it through.
I counted my steps back like I count heads at dusk.
A scattered mind is hard to gather. I managed it enough to get home.
The village gate felt like a pen after a long, bad storm.
I made it back with my heart running ahead of me.
Keeping calm is easier when no one is shouting. I did my best anyway.
I reached home and only then remembered to breathe properly.
A flock knows danger before pride admits it. I listen to the woolly experts.
Dye work teaches patience. So does convincing sheep that the gate is not a puzzle.
Warm beds start as quiet animals and careful hands.

Back to turning wool into warmth, then.
Back to woolwork before the work notices I stopped.
I have thread to tend and daylight to spend.
Fine. I will smooth this wool down for now.
Fine. I will set this down before it gets heavier.
